items.title: Player interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2012
items.q: he played with Guitar Slim for many years

ctx.x: Jazz historians, when you’re talking about that exact thing, about their individual sound, they sometimes say that they were rebelling against the more straightforward European approach to music. Do you think that’s true?

I don’t think that it was a rebellion against — I don’t think it was a rebellion at all. I think it was just, as I said before, just an extension of themselves. I think that because of the unique individual, the uniqueness of everything about New Orleans, the diverse cultures and everything, it allowed people to be individuals. And then that was just as a result of that. They would take that music and, as an older gentleman, a piano player, Lawrence Cotton I played with and he’s like a father to me, he played…

Well you know, sometimes I think in jazz or in a lot of fields it’s easier to write about things that are negative or that need to be fixed. And recently I’ve been reading articles about jazz and race, jazz and gender, jazz and generations. Is there any issues with that in the current New Orleans music scene?
